title: A Space-Launch Crash Is Coming
gist: Anik Joshi warns of a coming launch-capacity crunch: SpaceX's Falcon 9, which flew almost half of global launches in 2025 with over 99% reliability, will stop selling rideshare missions after 2028 and retire around 2030. Competitors (Blue Origin, ULA, Arianespace, Rocket Lab, Firefly, Stoke Space, Isar Aerospace) lack the scale and reliability to replace it, and high capex in a high-rate environment makes the build-out hard, implying higher costs for the commercial space industry.

insights.claim: The Falcon 9 has flown roughly 700 times — the most of any active launch vehicle — with a success rate above 99 percent, and in 2025 accounted for almost half of all rocket launches globally.
insights.so_what: The commercial space sector rests on a single supplier, a concentration risk for satellite and space companies.
insights.quote: In 2025, the Falcon 9 was used for almost half of all rocket launches globally.
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: The U.S. commercial launch industry is essentially SpaceX, and both U.S. government and many international customers also depend on it.
insights.so_what: Any SpaceX capacity reallocation ripples across commercial, government and foreign space programs.
insights.quote: The U.S. commercial launch industry is basically SpaceX
insights.locator: SpaceX has been synonymous with both launch
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: The large SpaceX IPO earlier in 2026 demonstrated deep public-market appetite for the space industry, around which a constellation of satellite and rocket companies has matured.
insights.so_what: Space equities are now a public-market theme exposed to launch-supply risk.
insights.locator: The commercial space market is booming
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Without decades of falling launch costs, much of the commercial space industry would have been dead on arrival.
insights.so_what: A reversal in launch costs threatens the business models of downstream space firms.
insights.locator: This has been, in turn, one of
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: SpaceX plans to stop flying Falcon 9 rideshare missions (slots sold per kilogram), with the last available in 2028; afterward direct purchases are only via the U.S. Defense Priorities and Allocations System for national-defense orders, and the rocket retires around 2030.
insights.so_what: Small-satellite operators lose their cheapest route to orbit from 2028, raising launch costs.
insights.quote: the last train from SpaceX leaves in 2028
insights.locator: While there are a few years left
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Every available Falcon 9 slot through 2028 is already booked and SpaceX keeps a waiting list.
insights.so_what: Launch capacity is already a binding constraint, giving pricing power to any provider with capacity.
insights.quote: Every single available Falcon 9 slot till 2028 is already booked
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: SpaceX's Falcon Heavy successor can carry other payloads but will not offer a routine rideshare program like Falcon 9's.
insights.so_what: Next-generation SpaceX vehicles do not replace the rideshare market.
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Blue Origin lost the only operational launch pad for New Glenn in an explosion earlier in 2026; it aims to have a pad ready by year-end, but NASA believes reaching scale will take longer.
insights.so_what: The most credible heavy-lift alternative is delayed.
insights.locator: After this, however, it’s not so clear
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: United Launch Alliance, the Boeing-Lockheed Martin joint venture, has historically been unreliable at reaching launch.
insights.so_what: Incumbent defense-aligned providers are unlikely to fill commercial demand on schedule.
insights.locator: After this, however, it’s not so clear
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Arianespace's Ariane 6 lacks a reusable first stage, has high costs and chronic schedule slips, and can manage about 10 launches a year versus SpaceX's 150+.
insights.so_what: Europe has no near-term substitute for SpaceX capacity.
insights.quote: Ariane 6, the company’s newest rocket, is capable of around 10 launches a year—SpaceX does north of 150
insights.locator: Across the pond, the picture isn’t much better.
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: New entrants show promise — Isar Aerospace reached orbit, Stoke Space raised a billion-dollar Series E for fully reusable rockets, plus Rocket Lab and Firefly — but all need time to build capacity.
insights.so_what: Launch startups that scale quickly could capture share and pricing power post-2028.
insights.locator: There are some bright new spots
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Building launch capacity requires massive capex during high inflation and likely soon-higher interest rates, making financing a challenging sell.
insights.so_what: Higher rates may slow the launch build-out and prolong the capacity gap.
insights.quote: massive capital expenditure spending during a time of high inflation as well as likely soon-to-be-higher interest rates
insights.locator: There are some bright new spots
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: No single company is likely to replace SpaceX's rideshare capacity, and fragmented providers cannot match its economies of scale, implying higher launch costs.
insights.so_what: Expect rising launch prices to compress margins for satellite operators after 2028.
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi

insights.claim: Because commercial and government space are intertwined, the Falcon 9 exit will have follow-on effects beyond launch costs, including on government launch reliability, and it is an open question who survives.
insights.so_what: A shakeout in commercial space firms is plausible as launch access tightens.
insights.quote: who survives what comes next is an open question
insights.locator: While this will have primary implications
insights.speaker: Anik Joshi
